results.question: Tell me about the lessons for AI engineers blog.
results.answer:
One of the most transferable lessons is to create an internal benchmark grounded in real tasks from your own environment, such as multi-file bug fixes, refactors, migrations, and test repair, rather than generic public benchmarks. [1]

Why Cursor’s Composer 2 gets close to Claude and Codex-class coding quality at much lower cost, and what AI engineers can learn from its specialization, reinforcement learning in real environments, and infra choices. [2]

Good coding agents also need to avoid wasted tool calls, preserve abstractions, recover from errors, and reach a good solution quickly; those qualities should be represented in the reward design. [3]

Cursor trained much closer to the environment where the model is supposed to work by incorporating speed, tool efficiency, concise interaction patterns, and the ability to maintain abstractions over longer horizons, rather than training a general chat model and only later wrapping it in tools. [4]

results.question: What does this mean: Composer 2 is not just a product launch; it is a useful blueprint for people building specialized AI systems?
results.answer:
Composer 2’s advantage comes from aligning training and product with real coding workflows, using environments that mirror actual IDE usage, file operations, semantic search, terminal access, tests, and background agents. [3]

The same infrastructure choices (MoE architecture, MXFP8 precision, PyTorch/Ray RL orchestration, KV-cache-aware serving) were chosen to reinforce the product loop of coding, testing, and iterating quickly. [4]

By pricing Composer 2 like a default tool and splitting into two SKUs with equal intelligence levels for lower cost/lower latency, Cursor shows that specialized training can be efficient without being a premium upsell. [1]

The lessons for AI engineers include optimizing for workflows rather than generic intelligence: pick a vertical where outcomes matter and align data, rewards, tools, evaluation, and product design around that loop. [5]

results.question: Why is it so efficient according to Tom?
results.answer:
Cursor trains and evaluates its model in environments that closely resemble the actual product, including real repositories, file operations, semantic search, terminal access, tests, and background agents, using RL rollouts scaled to hundreds of thousands of sandboxed coding environments. [2]

Composer 2 uses infrastructure choices like MoE architecture, MXFP8 precision, PyTorch and Ray-style RL orchestration, and KV-cache-aware serving to reduce compute and make long iterative sessions cheaper to run. [3]

Composer 2’s advantage comes from stack alignment: a narrow domain focus on programming tasks, shared runtime across training and product (the same environments powering RL also power the product experience), and evaluation tied to coding-heavy suites like CursorBench, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and SWE-bench Multilingual. [4]

The efficiency stems from aligning data, rewards, tools, evaluation, and product design around a specific workflow loop (coding, testing, iterating quickly) rather than chasing generic general-purpose intelligence. [5]

results.question: Why does the SQL explorer pattern inspect metadata before generating SQL?
results.answer:
Most text-to-SQL demos show the happy path, but real production environments are messier because table names can be ambiguous and columns store codes instead of labels. [1]

The naive pipeline (user question → LLM → SQL → execute → answer) fails in production for predictable reasons: wrong column assumptions, wrong table selection, and wrong join logic, all without runtime errors. [2]

The explorer pattern forces the agent to do grounded discovery before generating SQL, giving disambiguation before execution, schema-grounded generation based on actual columns and types, traceable reasoning steps, and security invariant enforcement even with complex query structures. [3]

Step 1 — Discover available data sources: the agent starts with list_tables (e.g., employees, attendance, approved_leave, absence_records) to identify join keys and likely candidates before any SQL is written. [4]

results.question: Why does Tom use COUNT(DISTINCT employee_id) instead of COUNT(*) in the example?
results.answer:
Tom uses COUNT(DISTINCT a.employee_id) instead of COUNT(*) to avoid overstating the number of absent employees when one employee has multiple absence records in the month, because COUNT(*) would count each row rather than each unique employee. [1]

The Explorer Pattern emphasizes generating SQL only after grounding source, schema, and filter values are confirmed to prevent wrong column assumptions (e.g., using a department name like 'Operations' instead of the internal code D042), wrong table selection, and incorrect join logic. [3]

Step 5 applies a security wrapper that rewrites table access by prepending deterministic security CTEs (e.g., _sec_employees) before executing base query SQL, making the generation robust across CTEs, self-joins, and complex aggregations. [2]

Step 3 resolves ambiguous user filter values by explicitly asking for distinct values of a column (e.g., department names) before mapping to internal codes like D042, preventing silent wrong answers when multiple departments match a search term. [4]

results.question: What is Dreamer?
results.answer:
Dreamer is a cloud platform where your main interface is a personal agent called Sidekick, surrounded by a growing ecosystem of other agents and tools. [1]

Dreamer is software running in secure, isolated VMs, with access to tools, data sources, and each other through a common OS layer. The Dreamer team describes it as 'an operating system for AI agents and agentic apps,' taking lessons from Android, ChromeOS, and other platforms they previously worked on. [2]

Under the hood, these agents are real software running in secure, isolated VMs, with physical data separation per user, giving a more robust foundation for serious personal software. The system is designed so that everything you build is intelligence-native by default, which the team frames as `software 3.0`. [4]

results.question: What role does Sidekick play in it?
results.answer:
Sidekick is a system-level agent that knows about all your other agents, tools, and data, and mediates how they work together. [4]

Sidekick is also important for safety and control: other agents do not just run wild; they go through Sidekick and the OS permission model when they want to use tools or access data. [3]

results.question: How is that different from a normal chatbot?
results.answer:
Every agent in Dreamer can expose functions to the rest of the system, turning agents into building blocks you can wire together instead of isolated chatbots that force manual steps. [1]

Dreamer is a cloud platform where your main interface is a personal agent called Sidekick, surrounded by an ecosystem of other agents and tools; it runs real software in secure, isolated VMs with access to tools, data sources, and each other through a common OS layer. [4]

Dreamer provides primitives for agents, tools, permissions, logging, a database, and serverless functions, effectively installing and composing intelligent apps rather than just prompts. [2]

results.question: Why did Tom shift to a unified explorer agent in the reliable SQL agents project?
results.answer:
Tom consolidated five domain plugins into one unified agent built on Semantic Kernel with Azure OpenAI, using an 'explorer-first' pattern that discovers what it needs before writing SQL instead of routing questions to pre-built domain generators. [3] [4]

The shift was motivated by preventing the agent from ever filtering on name columns directly and improving reliability through stronger instruction-following and contextual reasoning after upgrading to GPT-5.2, which reduced hallucinated column names and improved multi-source join handling. [2]

The unified explorer-first toolset exposes a small focused set of functions: List Tables, Get Schema, Get Distinct Values, Resolve Name to Code (translating human-readable entity names into internal identifier codes), and others for the orchestrator. [4]

results.question: What would he do differently from day one?
results.answer:
If starting fresh, I would start with data modernization (unified schema design, quality constraints, and proper join performance via a data lake rather than fighting a fragmented linked-view structure throughout development). [3]

Add a semantic model early: a semantic model abstracts raw schema into named business entities, documented relationships, and reusable measures. In a mature warehouse this comes naturally, but even a versioned metadata contract is enough to give the agent stable semantics instead of rediscovering structure at query time. [3]

Define agent-friendly metadata upfront: column descriptions, join keys, and domain rules should live in source control from the start — not discovered iteratively through production failures. [3]

The core patterns (explorer-first toolset, Security CTE Prefix, read-only validator) are available as an open-source reference implementation at github.com/tomvsaji/text-to-sql-agent using LangGraph and a SQLite demo database rather than Semantic Kernel and SQL Server. [4]
